_readme: All game content lives here. First-draft content written 2026-11-20 for the instructor to edit; cards carry a 'reading' so the debrief can trace them. Condition syntax used everywhere (appears_when, when, condition): a list of terms that must ALL hold; a term 'a|b' holds if ANY of a or b is active; an empty list or ['any'] always holds. Indicator ids used in effects: reach, burden, fiscal, political. Equity is NOT an effect column: it is 100 minus the gap between the best- and worst-served target group, so to move Equity use group_multipliers (on options) or group_reach (on modifiers and cards). Numbers are first-draft and should be tuned after one playtest.

setting.transition_warning: Cases already in the pipeline were decided under the old rule. Expect one quarter of mixed outcomes.
setting.purpose_template: The {council} finds that {cs}. The {program} aims at {gg}, chiefly through {il}.

fit_definitions.coherence: Coherence: do the goals agree with each other, from the governing aim down to the objectives and settings?
fit_definitions.consistency: Consistency: do the means reinforce each other, from the approach down to the tools and the fine print?
fit_definitions.congruence: Congruence: at each level, can the means plausibly deliver the goals?

setting.fit_note: Fit is about whether the design hangs together. It is not the same as whether the design works. A design can be all green and still help almost no one.

budget.note: The appropriation is total_dollars, tracked internally as a percentage. Spend per quarter = quarter_spend_at_reach50 (percent) x (Reach / 50) x the product of the 'cost' multipliers on active options. The Budget panel drains toward that figure as the quarter's cases are worked. An applicant outcome whose result is in paid_results shows the household's payment: case_dollars_per_month x months of duration x the cap's cost multiplier (x 'pays' if the outcome sets one). A choice or outcome with a 'budget' key in its effects moves the appropriation by that many percentage points for real. When the remaining budget cannot cover the quarter, applicant cases from a point onward are turned away. Tune after one playtest.
budget.dry_text: This quarter's appropriation is spent. The application is held until new money arrives.
budget.dry_headline: {newspaper}: 'Housing program runs out of money in week nine.'

setting.debrief_instructions: Download the log (the button below) and write your answers at the bottom of that file. Paste the whole file into your memo as the appendix.

groups.name: Working families with an eviction notice
Undocumented or mixed-status households
groups.construction: deviants in the political frame: no power

indicators.name: Reach
indicators.description: Share of eligible households that actually receive aid

indicators.name: Burden
indicators.description: Learning, compliance and psychological cost borne by applicants (higher is worse)

indicators.name: Equity
indicators.description: 100 minus the gap between the best- and worst-served target group

indicators.name: Fiscal integrity
indicators.description: Inverse of improper payments and cost overrun

indicators.name: Political support
indicators.description: Council and press standing; renewal odds

sub.template: {v} in 10 applicants gave up before finishing the form.

lines.text: The auditor has nothing to report.
Money is leaving faster than the paperwork.
The Mayor can run on this.
Council members quote your own ordinance back at you.

endings.title: The program is renewed. So are you.
endings.text: Council voted {votes} of 5 to renew. The Mayor has asked you to run the department. You told the council that {cs}; after two quarters of cases, the council tells that story as its own.

endings.title: Renewed, on probation.
endings.text: Council voted {votes} of 5 to renew for one year, with conditions and a monthly report. You told the council that {cs}. Half the council is no longer sure, and the other half is watching the budget.

endings.title: The Mayor has accepted your resignation.
endings.text: Council support fell to {votes} of 5 after {newspaper}'s third story. The program will be redesigned by your successor. You told the council that {cs}; the council now asks why the fine print punished the people the ordinance named.

choices.name: Problem
choices.prompt: What kind of problem is this?
choices.lead: Evictions are up 40%. Your answer decides what kind of program the council believes it adopted.
choices.note: Causal stories carry no direct effects. They work through the implied aim and approach, the modifiers, and the cards that react to them (Stone 2012 ch. 2).

options.label: Market failure
options.tooltip: Rents outran wages. Nobody did anything wrong; the market stopped clearing for the bottom third. You'll want money in the system, not rules.
options.purpose: rents have outrun wages and the market no longer clears for low-income households

options.label: Landlord behavior
options.tooltip: Filings are up because filing is cheap and profitable. If the problem is landlord behavior, you're going to want teeth.
options.purpose: opportunistic eviction filings by landlords are driving displacement

options.label: Tenant behavior
options.tooltip: Payment habits, information gaps, people who don't know help exists. Fix the household and the filings follow.
options.purpose: household payment habits and information gaps leave tenants exposed

options.label: Structural shortage
options.tooltip: There aren't enough units. Any program that pays rent treats a symptom, and the Chief of Staff will say so.
options.purpose: the city lacks affordable units and every rental program treats a symptom

options.label: Housing as a right
options.tooltip: Nobody gets evicted for want of a few months' rent.

options.label: Market stabilization
options.tooltip: Keep landlords renting and tenants paying.
options.purpose: stabilizing the rental market for landlords and tenants

options.label: Fiscal prudence
options.tooltip: Spend only what is needed, only on those who qualify, and prove it.

options.label: Neighborhood preservation
options.tooltip: Keep Rosario Heights looking like Rosario Heights.
options.purpose: preserving the city's neighborhoods and the people in them

options.label: Coercive / regulatory
options.tooltip: Rules, duties, penalties.

options.label: Financial / market
options.tooltip: Pay for the outcome you want.

options.label: Communicative / voluntary
options.tooltip: Information, persuasion, hotlines.

options.label: Network / co-production
options.tooltip: Work through the nonprofits and tenant groups that already know these households.

choices.name: Objectives
choices.lead: Any pair is in tension with itself. The evaluators will find it. Each is a promise with a target.

options.label: Cut evictions 30%
options.kept_if: at least 50% of working families with an eviction notice are helped by the end
options.tooltip: The headline the Mayor wants. In this game it means reaching half the families with a notice in hand.

options.label: Reach 70% of eligible households
options.kept_if: the Households helped dial is 70% or more at the end
options.tooltip: Take-up is the whole game here. Every form field is an enemy of this objective.

options.label: Keep fraud and error under 3%
options.kept_if: no more than 3 cents of every dollar paid out went to households that did not qualify or were paid twice
options.tooltip: The Budget Office's objective: almost no money to people who did not qualify. Every form field is a friend of this one.

options.label: Keep small landlords paid
options.kept_if: at least 60% of small landlords whose tenants fell behind actually receive the rent they are owed
options.tooltip: Owners of one to four units sell to big operators when the rent stops coming. Make sure most of them get paid, so they keep renting.

options.label: Decide applications in 14 days
options.kept_if: fewer than 5 in 10 applicants give up before finishing (Burden 45 or less at the end)
options.tooltip: Speed. Works against every review step you add downstream. In this game it means keeping burden low.

choices.name: Payment
choices.lead: The council will fund one instrument mix.
choices.note: First-draft numbers. Direction follows Schneider & Ingram 1990 (tools assume a theory of who complies and why).

options.label: Pay the landlord directly
options.tooltip: Pay the landlord, close the case. Landlords love it; mixed-status families won't apply if the landlord has to sign.

options.label: Pay the tenant
options.tooltip: Pay the household. Dignity and flexibility; also the occasional payment that never reaches the landlord.

options.label: Payment plus counseling
options.tooltip: Rent plus a mandatory session with a housing counselor. Changes behavior, if behavior was the problem; adds an appointment nobody asked for.

options.label: Campaign, hotline, small grants
options.tooltip: Bus ads, a hotline and emergency grants. Cheap and visible. Information alone does not pay anyone's rent.

choices.name: Implementer
choices.lead: The council will fund one implementer.
choices.note: First-draft numbers. Direction follows May 2012 (implementers bring their own values) and Busetti & Dente 2018 (contractors cream-skim).

options.label: City housing department
options.tooltip: Our own people. They know the rules, and they are already behind on last year's program.

options.label: Community nonprofits
options.tooltip: The organizations the Okafor-Mendez family already trusts. Reach goes up where we need it most; the paper trail gets thinner.

options.label: Private contractor
options.tooltip: Fast, measurable, paid per completed case. Guess which cases they complete first.

options.label: Online portal only
options.tooltip: Cheapest by far. Harold B., 74, does not own a smartphone.

choices.name: Income threshold
choices.prompt: Who is poor enough to qualify?
choices.lead: The council has delegated this to you for one adjustment.
choices.note: First-draft numbers. Set by council in the base game; opened by the Q2 unlock.

options.label: 50% of area median income
options.tooltip: The poorest third. Many working families with a notice in hand will be just over the line.

options.label: 80% of area median income
options.tooltip: The conventional line. Nobody will praise it and nobody will attack it.

options.label: 120% of area median income
options.tooltip: Nearly universal. The Budget Office will ask why a nurse is getting rent money.

choices.name: Benefit cap
choices.prompt: How much per household per month?
choices.lead: The council has delegated this to you for one adjustment.
choices.note: First-draft numbers. Set by council in the base game; opened by the Q2 unlock.

options.label: Low cap
options.tooltip: Covers rent in Castelldefels Flats, not in Bayside Terrace.

options.label: Mid cap
options.tooltip: Covers the median rent. Fine.

options.label: High cap
options.tooltip: Covers any rent in the city. Fewer households served, each fully.

choices.name: Duration
choices.note: Set by council in the base game.

options.label: 3 months
options.tooltip: A bridge. Households come back next quarter if nothing else changed.

options.label: 6 months
options.tooltip: Half a year of stability. The usual.

options.label: 12 months
options.tooltip: A year. Fewer households, more stability each.

choices.name: Application window
choices.note: Set by council in the base game.

options.label: Rolling
options.tooltip: Apply any day. Easy for applicants, hard to budget.

options.label: Two fixed rounds
options.tooltip: Two deadlines a year. The eviction hearing does not wait for the next round.

choices.name: Eligibility route
choices.note: Not in the design document's Section 4 table; added so the Section 5 modifiers and the cards that mention 'universal', 'priority tiers' and 'landlord-initiated' eligibility have something to point at. Set by council in the base game.

options.label: Universal (any at-risk household)
options.tooltip: Anyone who says they are at risk may apply. The line is long.

options.label: Priority tiers
options.tooltip: Serve the most urgent first. The tiering itself takes a review step.

options.label: Written eviction notice required
options.tooltip: A notice in hand proves need. We help only after the landlord has started.

options.label: Landlord-initiated
options.tooltip: The landlord applies for the tenant. The tenant who never hears about it is not counted anywhere.

choices.name: Documentation
choices.lead: Caseworkers will apply this to every file.
choices.note: Effects from Section 5 of the design document, with the standard option given its own small costs. Group multipliers follow Moynihan et al. 2015: documentation burden falls hardest on those with the least paper.

options.label: Self-attestation
options.tooltip: Sign here that it's true. Everyone finishes the form; some of them should not have.

options.label: Standard documents
options.tooltip: Lease, ID, one proof of income. The form every other city uses.

options.label: Full verification
options.tooltip: We've caught every fraud case we've ever had this way. We've also lost about a third of applicants before they finish the form.

choices.name: Enforcement
choices.prompt: When do we check, and what if we were wrong?
choices.lead: This is what the auditor will test.
choices.note: First-draft numbers. Direction follows Bardach App. B (improper payments) and Moynihan et al. 2015 (review steps are burden).

options.label: Trust and audit later
options.tooltip: Pay first, sample later. Fast money, and the auditor's sample will find something.

options.label: Review before payment
options.tooltip: Every file reviewed before a dollar moves. Clean books; the hearing is in eleven days.

options.label: Pay fast, claw back errors
options.tooltip: Pay fast, then send letters demanding money back. One of those letters will go to a data-entry error.

choices.name: Form length
choices.note: Set by council in the base game.

options.label: One page
options.tooltip: Fits on one side. Some questions go unasked.

options.label: Full packet
options.tooltip: Eleven pages and a checklist. A lot goes unanswered.

choices.name: Appeal window
choices.note: Set by council in the base game.

options.label: No appeal
options.tooltip: A decision is a decision.

options.label: 14 days
options.tooltip: Two weeks to object. Reasonable.

options.label: 60 days
options.tooltip: Two months to object. The caseload never quite closes.

fit_rules.explanation: Fiscal prudence, reach 70% and a near-universal threshold cannot all be pursued at once.
Fiscal prudence as the governing aim and take-up as an objective pull the goals column apart. One of them will be sacrificed quietly, at the level of the fine print.
A rights frame tolerates error in favor of access; a 3% error ceiling does not. The goals column points two ways.
Market stabilization and stabilizing landlord receipts are the same goal at two levels.
Housing as a right and reaching 70% of the eligible are the same commitment at two levels.
You named a shortage of units as the problem and promised to cut evictions with rent money. The story and the objective describe different problems.
Co-production, community implementers and trust-based documentation reinforce each other.
A trust-based network with every file reviewed before payment: the means undercut each other.
A communicative approach paired with pre-payment review is inconsistent means.
Persuasion at the top, clawback letters at the bottom. The Tenant Coalition notices first.
A financial approach delivered as direct payment is consistent means.
A regulatory approach delivered through bus ads and a hotline. The means at the top and the bottom belong to different theories of why people comply.
Co-production needs partners. A portal has users.
Cutting evictions 30% with a campaign and a hotline: the means cannot deliver the goal.
fit_rules.citation: Van Geet et al. 2021; Schneider & Ingram 1990

fit_rules.explanation: A 70% reach objective paired with full verification is incongruent goal and means.
Reaching 70% through a portal only: the households you most need to reach are the ones least likely to log in.
Stabilizing landlord receipts by paying landlords directly: the means fit the goal.
Market stabilization through financial instruments is congruent at the macro level.
An error ceiling of 3% with self-attested applications: the means cannot deliver the goal, by construction.
A 14-day decision with every file reviewed before payment: speed and verification trade against each other inside the same queue.
A right backed by enforceable duties on landlords: the macro means fit the macro goal.

modifiers.explanation: Full verification through a portal only: the digital-divide cost falls on the elderly and mixed-status households.
Information alone does not move resource-constrained groups.
Trust networks raise take-up among mixed-status households but thin the audit trail.
Serving contenders: landlords are paid and happy; tenants who were never asked are not served.
Pre-payment review plus priority tiers: the prioritized group waits longest.
The contractor cream-skims the easy cases and leaves the rest to the clawback letters.
The council asks why you are paying the people you said were the problem.
The program cannot fix what it did not aim at: Reach cannot exceed 60.
Inconsistent means: persuasion at the top and clawback letters at the bottom.
You told the council landlords were the problem, then wrote them the checks. The Coalition's press release writes itself.

fields.Documents: Lease [x]  ID [x]  Proof of income [ ] (employer pays cash)

outcomes.text: No acceptable proof of income. Her hearing goes ahead.
Approved on attestation. Payment issued before the hearing.

fields.Headline: Mother of two evicted while city program sat on 60% of its budget

default.text: Your office is asked for comment by noon.

fields.Income: Social Security; proof is a paper letter
fields.Access: No smartphone, no email, no car

outcomes.text: He asks a neighbor's grandson for help. The grandson is at college. The application is never completed.
A volunteer at the neighborhood center completes the form with him over coffee.
The contractor's intake line is open 9 to 5. He is on hold for 40 minutes, twice.

default.text: Approved after a second trip downtown on the bus.

fields.Status: Mixed. Afraid to put a name on any form that goes to City Hall.

outcomes.text: Approved through the parish housing desk. No file leaves the building.
The parish desk helps with the form, then asks for a lease in their own name. They do not have one. They stop coming.

default.text: The household never applies. This case is visible only in who got help.

cards.title: Dana P., owner of three units

fields.Situation: Two tenants behind, both good tenants for six years
fields.Request: Applies on their behalf with both leases and a cover letter

outcomes.text: Both arrears paid directly within the week. She tells the landlord association.
She is sent a brochure and the hotline number. She lists both units on the market.

default.text: Told the tenants must apply themselves. One does; the other is embarrassed and never does.

cards.title: Caseworker query: the month-to-month lease

fields.Situation: Lease expired last month; she is now month-to-month
fields.Asks: Approve, deny, or ask the landlord for a letter?

cards.reading: Week 7 (why designers write the policy text)

choices.label: Approve
choices.text: The caseworker notes the interpretation for the file. Every month-to-month tenant in the city now qualifies.

choices.label: Deny
choices.text: A strict reading of 'current lease.' She has a hearing in nine days and no lease to show.

choices.label: Request a landlord letter (adds 2 weeks)
choices.text: The landlord who is evicting her is asked to write a letter confirming she lives there.

cards.title: Ruth and Amadou K., retired

fields.Income: Two pensions; one is paid quarterly and looks like a windfall on paper

cards.reading: Moynihan et al. 2015 (psychological costs); Bardach App. B

outcomes.text: The quarterly pension triggers a manual review. The review takes 24 days. The hearing was in 21.
Paid in four days. In week nine a letter arrives demanding repayment because the pension was counted twice. It was the city's error.
Paid in four days. Nobody ever looks at the pension statement.

fields.Situation: Hours cut in March; two months behind
fields.Constraint: Works 6am to 4pm, six days a week

outcomes.text: The counseling session is Tuesdays at 2pm. He cannot leave the floor. He withdraws rather than lose the shift.
Paid directly. He pays the landlord the same afternoon.
His landlord is paid. He finds out from the landlord.
He calls the hotline on his break. The small grant covers one of the two months.

cards.title: Mr. Esposito, one unit above his shop

fields.Situation: His tenant was approved for aid last month
fields.Complaint: The rent has still not arrived

cards.reading: Schneider & Ingram 1990 (who the tool assumes will comply)

outcomes.text: The tenant used the money to fix the car she drives to work. He files for eviction anyway.
The payment reached him directly. He withdraws the filing.
His tenant received a brochure. He received nothing.

default.text: The payment reached him after the counseling session was completed.

cards.title: Lucia, 16, and her mother

fields.Scene: Lucia is translating the application for her mother at the kitchen table
fields.Missing: A document the household does not have

cards.reading: May 2012 (implementers bring their own values); Moynihan et al. 2015

outcomes.text: Incomplete file closed after 10 days per contract. The letter is in English.
A form letter requests the missing document. It is in English. Lucia translates it; they do not have the document.
A caseworker from the neighborhood center visits and accepts a school enrollment letter instead.
The upload step rejects a photo of the letter. There is no second try.

cards.title: Mrs. Delacroix, 81

fields.Situation: Two months behind after a hospital stay
fields.Income: She forgets to list a small annuity. With it, she is over the line.

cards.reading: Bardach App. B (improper payments are not always fraud)

outcomes.text: Approved on attestation. The annuity is never mentioned. The payment is improper, and she is housed.
The bank statements show the annuity. Denied. She is 81 and three weeks from a hearing.
One proof of income was enough. The annuity surfaces at audit in six months.

fields.Situation: Moved in with a cousin the week the notice came
fields.Request: Pay the arrears to the old landlord so the eviction never goes on their record
fields.The rule says: Aid stabilizes a tenancy. There is no tenancy.

choices.label: Pay the arrears to clear the record
choices.text: Paid. The eviction record is withdrawn. The program has just paid for a household that no longer needs housing.

choices.label: Deny: no tenancy to stabilize
choices.text: Denied. The record stands. The next landlord sees it.

choices.label: Pay it toward a deposit on a new unit
choices.text: Not in the rules. The caseworker makes it work. The auditor will not like the paperwork.

cards.title: Grandview Holdings LLC, four units

fields.Situation: Filed on all four tenants the day the program was announced
fields.Request: Four applications, four leases, one cover letter

cards.reading: Stone 2012 ch. 2 (landlord behavior as a causal story)

choices.label: Pay all four
choices.text: Four tenants stay housed. The landlord's strategy worked, and every owner on the block saw it work.

choices.label: Refuse until the filings are withdrawn
choices.text: The landlord withdraws two filings and proceeds with two. Two tenants are housed, two are not.

choices.label: Pay, and refer the landlord to code enforcement
choices.text: Four tenants housed. Code enforcement finds three violations. The landlord association calls the Mayor.

cards.title: The Nguyen-Alvarez household

fields.Situation: One month behind; landlord is willing to sign anything that gets him paid
fields.Status: Mixed. Will not put their own names on a city form.

cards.reading: Schneider & Ingram 1990 (the same tool reaches different people)

outcomes.text: The landlord applies and signs. The household is never named on any form. Paid.
Counseling requires photo ID at the door. They do not go.
The payment would go to a bank account in their name. They do not have one and do not want one.

default.text: They are given a hotline number by a neighbor. They do not call it.

cards.title: Mr. and Mrs. Okonkwo, 70 and 68

fields.Situation: Rent rose 22% at renewal; three weeks behind

cards.reading: Howlett 2009 (settings decide who is inside the line)

outcomes.text: Inside the line. Paid.
Four points over the income line. The caseworker apologizes. They sell the car.

cards.title: Priya and Dev S., one child

fields.Situation: Hearing in two weeks; rent is 40% above the city median

outcomes.text: Covered in full. Three months of a Bayside Terrace rent.
The cap covers less than half the arrears. The landlord proceeds. The city has paid for an eviction.

default.text: The mid cap covers two-thirds. The landlord accepts it, this time.

fields.Practice: Approving self-attested cases under 1,000 without review, to clear the backlog

choices.label: Endorse it
choices.text: The informal rule continues. Nobody writes it down.

choices.label: Stop it
choices.text: Reviews resume. The backlog grows. She starts looking at other postings.

choices.label: Formalize it as a rule
choices.text: A written fast-track for small claims. The auditor is told.

fields.Incomplete files: 4% approved; mostly families and mixed-status households

default.text: The report is filed. The pattern continues. The contractor's invoice is on time.

fields.Asks: Can a utility bill count as proof of residence for a mixed-status family with no lease in its own name?

choices.label: Yes
choices.text: Utility bills count. Three more families apply the next week. None of the bills are in the applicants' names.

choices.label: No
choices.text: The family withdraws. The caseworker stops asking and starts deciding.

outcomes.text: The 14-day objective is missed by nine days. The memo asks for four hires the budget does not have.

default.text: Processing time noted. Nobody is hired.

outcomes.text: Full verification needs six uploads. Most of the 65+ applicants stop at the second.
One checkbox. Abandonment is low, and so is the audit trail.

default.text: Three uploads. A third of the elderly applicants never finish.

fields.Request: Drop the appeal step. "It adds eight days per file and we are paid per completed case."

choices.label: Agree
choices.text: Appeals end for contractor-handled files. Completions rise. So do complaints.

choices.label: Refuse
choices.text: The contractor's completion rate drops and the invoice does not.

cards.title: Clawback unit report

fields.Of which: 11 went to households that were correctly paid. Data entry.

cards.reading: Moynihan et al. 2015 (psychological costs); Bardach App. B

choices.label: Cancel the 11 and apologize in writing
choices.text: Eleven apologies. The Ledger prints one of them.

choices.label: Let the letters stand; they can appeal
choices.text: Four of the eleven appeal. Seven pay money they did not owe.

choices.label: Pause all clawbacks this quarter
choices.text: No letters. The auditor notes that recovery has stopped.

fields.Offer: Pre-screen tenants and submit bundled applications

choices.label: Accept
choices.text: Bundled applications arrive the next week. The tenants in them are the ones landlords chose.

choices.label: Decline
choices.text: A polite letter back. The association's newsletter is less polite.

choices.label: Accept, with tenant consent required
choices.text: Fewer bundles, each with a tenant's signature.

cards.title: Council hearing, Committee on Housing

fields.Question: Why has the program spent 40% of its budget and reached 15% of eligible households?

cards.reading: Stone 2012 ch. 5 (efficiency as a contested criterion)

outcomes.text: "You built a wall of paper and called it a program."
"You ran ads."
"You have reached a lot of households. The auditor says a tenth of them should not have been reached."

default.text: Your deputy answers. The clip is not flattering.

outcomes.text: Published: duplicates paid without review. Extrapolated citywide on page 2.
No finding. The review queue is now 19 days long.
Letters to 3 households. One was a data-entry error; the Ledger has her name.

fields.Angle: Monthly cap compared with median rents by neighborhood

outcomes.text: "City aid covers two-thirds of the rent in Bayside Terrace."
"City pays Old Port penthouse rents."

default.text: The numbers are unremarkable. No story runs. The reporter keeps the spreadsheet.

fields.Proposal: Two years' city residence for eligibility, "so Messiland money stays with Messiland families"

choices.label: Support it
choices.text: The amendment passes committee. Proof of two years' residence is a new document.

choices.label: Oppose it
choices.text: The amendment fails. The council member remembers, and chairs the renewal vote.

choices.label: Propose one year instead
choices.text: One year passes. Everyone is slightly unhappy.

fields.Statement: Twenty owners of one to four units cannot wait for payments and are selling to a regional operator.

outcomes.text: Six buildings sold this quarter. The operator does not accept city aid.
Direct payment keeps most of them in the market.

default.text: Comment filed. Two buildings sell.

fields.Subject: The ordinance's statement of the problem

outcomes.text: "The city has decided the problem with evictions is the people being evicted." The clip runs for two days.
"For once a program names the problem." The landlord association holds its own press conference the next day.
"The Mayor says there are no apartments. We agree. Where is the housing plan?"

default.text: "Rents went up and wages did not. Fine. Who is paying?" The story is about the budget.

fields.Impact: 400 households newly at risk. Applications double.

outcomes.text: The quarter's quota cannot be met. Hearings come before decisions.
Quota met. Some of the new approvals will not survive an audit.

default.text: Processing slows but holds.

cards.title: Notice from the State Housing Fund

choices.label: Comply
choices.text: Mixed-status households are no longer eligible. The state is satisfied.

choices.label: Seek a waiver (50% chance, one quarter)
choices.text: Payments to affected households pause while the state decides.

choices.label: Fund them from city reserves
choices.text: A separate line in the city budget. The council notices the line.

fields.Decision: Approved. Paused payments resume with back pay.

default.text: Eligibility restored.

fields.Decision: Denied. Mixed-status households lose eligibility, one quarter late.

default.text: Eligibility ends.

outcomes.text: Four improper payments in your sample. A corrective action plan is requested.
Two attestations could not be supported. A corrective action plan is requested.

default.text: No findings. The letter is one paragraph.

fields.Impact: Portal down six days in the month's final week

choices.label: Extend the deadline a week
choices.text: The deadline moves. Budget forecasts slip.

choices.label: Open a paper line at City Hall
choices.text: A line forms on Plaza Diez. The Ledger photographs it.

choices.label: Hold the deadline

fields.Finding: Every priority file needs a tier review before the payment review. The prioritized group waits longest.

default.text: The queue inverts the priority.

evaluators.name: Messiland Budget Office
evaluators.template: Budget Office, Q{q}. We read the fine print, not the speeches. Fraud and error stand at {improper}% of spending; {budget} of the appropriation remains. {verdict} The files that drove these numbers: {cards}.

verdicts.text: The calibrations are doing their job. Hold them against the pressure that is coming from the Coalition.
Documentation or enforcement is leaking. Tighten one of them before the state audit, not both.
Money is going out faster than the paperwork can justify. The problem is in the fine print, at your desk, and it is fixable there.

evaluators.name: Tenant Coalition of Messiland
evaluators.template: Tenant Coalition, Q{q}. You promised {objectives}. You reached {helped}% of eligible households, and {worst_pct}% of {worst_group}. {verdict} What we are hearing in the neighborhoods: {cards}.

verdicts.text: The program is reaching the people it was written for, including the ones no office ever reaches.
The objectives were the right ones. The tools are not carrying them to Rosario Heights or the Old Port.
Whoever this program is for, it is not the households being evicted this month. Either the objectives were wrong or the tools cannot reach them.

evaluators.name: Mayor's Chief of Staff
evaluators.template: Chief of Staff, Q{q}. Your ordinance told the council: "{purpose}" Council stands at {votes} of 5. Promises: {promises}. {verdict} What the council remembers: {cards}.

verdicts.text: The story holds. Council members are repeating it as their own, which is the only test that matters.
The story is wobbling. Two members quoted your purpose statement back at you with a question mark.
The frame did not survive the cases. Council is asking whether the problem was ever what you said it was.

briefings.title: How this works
lines: You are the Mayor's analyst in {city}. Evictions are up 40%. The council wants a rental assistance program by Friday.
First you write the ordinance: six questions, one at a time. Your answers fill the grid on the left.
Then you run the program for three quarters. Each quarter you work eight cases. Your rules decide most of them; on two you decide yourself.
After each quarter a different evaluator writes to you. They judge different things, so they will disagree.
Your two objectives are promises. Every promise you miss at the end costs you council support.
The budget is fixed. Generous rules spend it faster, and when it runs out, applicants are turned away.
Before each new quarter you may redesign documentation and enforcement. Nothing else can change.
At the end the council votes on renewal, and on you.
The three lights under the grid show whether your design hangs together. The three dials on the right show whether it works. These are not the same thing.

briefings.title: The Ordinance
briefings.text: Evictions are up 40%. The {council} wants the {program} designed by Friday. Six choices are yours; the rest is set by council.

briefings.title: The ordinance passed
briefings.text: The council adopted your design. The program opens Monday. You will run it for three quarters; a different evaluator writes after each.

briefings.title: Quarter 1
briefings.text: Applications are arriving at the {mayors_office} and at every neighborhood center. Work the cases. The Budget Office writes first.
briefings.redesign: Redesign. Documentation and enforcement are yours to change before Quarter 2. Everything else is locked.

briefings.title: Quarter 2
briefings.text: The Tenant Coalition is counting who got help, by neighborhood.
briefings.redesign: Redesign. Documentation and enforcement are yours to change before Quarter 3, the final quarter.

briefings.title: Quarter 2
briefings.text: The Tenant Coalition is counting who got help, by neighborhood. The council has delegated the fine print to you: income threshold and benefit cap are now open too.
briefings.redesign: Redesign. Documentation, enforcement, income threshold and benefit cap are yours to change before Quarter 3, the final quarter.

briefings.title: Quarter 3
briefings.text: Final quarter. The Chief of Staff will judge whether your story survived, and the council votes on renewal when it ends.

briefings.title: Quarter 3
briefings.text: Final quarter. The Chief of Staff will judge whether your story survived, and the council votes on renewal when it ends.

debrief_prompts: Name one case whose result surprised you. Which of your six choices produced that result?
Which evaluator's memo was hardest to dismiss, and what does that tell you about whose criteria you were implicitly designing for?

The game's model assumes certain things about how applicants, caseworkers and landlords behave. Name one such assumption, say whether it is defensible, and say what a real policy designer, or an AI tool, would need to know to check it.

Your fit lights and your results probably disagreed at some point. Which would you rather have had, a fitted design or an effective one, and what does the disagreement tell you about the level at which your design went wrong?
